{{< iconify clarity group-solid >}} Bayes Rule: Do Exclamation Marks in Headlines help define fake news? Let us replicate the initial analysis in Chapter 2 of the book *Bayes Rule* by Mine Dogucu et al. The goal is to update our beliefs about the probability of a coin being fair given new evidence. Let us first define our events: 1. Event F: News item is *fake* or *real*. p = c(0.4, 0.6) for fake and real news, respectively. These are our ***prior*** probabilities. 2. Event E: News item has an exclamation mark in the headline. Looking at the ***data***, we find that : ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} data(fake_news, package = "bayesrules") fake_news %>% glimpse() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} fake_news %>% count(title_has_excl) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: We can see that 60 out of 150 news items are fake, and 90 are real. Of the fake news, 16 have an exclamation mark in the title, while only 2 of the real news have an exclamation mark in the title. We can summarize this information in a contingency table: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} vcd::structable(type ~ title_has_excl, data = fake_news) %>% addmargins() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` type title_has_excl fake real Sum FALSE 44 88 132 TRUE 16 2 18 Sum 60 90 150 ``` ::: ::: And the ***likelihoods*** of the events are: - $P(E | F)$: Exclamation given Fake: 16/60 = 0.267 - $P(E | F_c)$: Exclamation given Real: 2/90 = 0.022 - $P(E_c | F )$: No Exclamation given Fake: 44/60 = 0.733 - $P(E_c | F_c)$: No Exclamation given Real: 88/90 = 0.978 Now we can use Bayes Rule to update our beliefs about the probability of a news item being fake given that it has an exclamation mark in the title: Here is the logic of that update: 1. We have P(F) = 0.4 and P(F_c) = 0.6 2. We have P(E | F) = 0.267 and P(E | F_c) = 0.022 3. We **want**: P(F | E) = P(E | F) * P(F) / P(E) Where P(E) is the total probability of E, which can be calculated as: $$ P(E) = P(E | F) * P(F) + P(E | F_c) * P(F_c) $$ 4.
